utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday. I'd like to greet Mr. Praljak, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic. I would also like to greet the Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer, his associates. I just am turning around to see whether Mr. Scott is there, but he's not. I also greet him, and the court reporter as well, and all the people assisting us in the courtroom, of course. We need to resume Mr. Praljak's testimony. I shall therefore give the floor to Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to you and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Good morning, General. We left off yesterday discussing the book "The Young Muslims," and you explained what the Young Muslims were. And you said that Sead Trhulj had written a book about them, so I'd like to ask you now to turn to page 3D41-0239, and in English the pages are 3D40-1561. The document number is 3D03540, and for Their Honours, it is to be found in binder number 3 among the book selection. General, let's begin.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two sentences on page 59 that I'd like to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: No, I just identified the book and the pages in the book, and we're now going to start by discussing it. And on page 3D41-0239, or in English 3D40-1561 and 3D40-1562, we have a chapter under the heading of "Alija Izetbegovic." Tell us, please, what do you want to point out in that section?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're just going to go through the excerpts which Alija Izetbegovic gave after the war to Sead Trhulj, and here at the beginning, briefly, he discusses the circumstances which led to the formation of the Young Muslim movement and organisation. And let me just say that the Muslim people had been left without a leader between the two world wars, and that during that period, during the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, a division of Bosnia had already been carried out, and that the Muslims left and went to Turkey in large numbers, and that these were all reasons for which they decided to form an organisation of that kind. And now we can go on to page 59.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That is 3D41-0241 in Croatian, and for the English it is 3D40-1562.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, when asked whether the programme documents -- what kind of programme documents the Young Muslims organisation had, he goes on to say that there was an item, a point about the unity of Muslims throughout the world, that's what it referred to, unity of Muslims worldwide, and how this could be practically realised, the practical realisation of Islam. And then the secret formula was "no comment," and Mr. Izetbegovic said that the Young Muslims always read this as the creation -- interpreted it as the creation of a large Muslim state. So that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next page. Would you give us the number.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's page 61.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That is 3D41-0242 for the Croatian and 3D40-1562 for the English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic says here -- he's speaking about the tragedy of the Muslim people, and he says that he could not join any party -- he could not join the partisans because the partisans were led by the Communists, which would have meant that the Muslims would have lost their soul if they had decided to join up with the Communists and partisans. And, on the other hand, you had the Nazi system which threatened them with physical extermination. And further on, when asked what role religion played in all this, he said that religion was of absolute importance, then and now. He is certain that Islam is the basis for Muslim identity in these parts, and he goes on to say that it is only Islam which can provide the Muslim people with meaning, and, That is my firm conviction, he says. There is nothing more I would like to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next page. It is 67, which in the Croatian version is 3D41-0249; and for the English it is 3D40-1563 and 3D40-1564.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, towards the end there, the author of the book asks him about 1983 and what prompted this group of people to go public that year. And there was a big trial against Young Muslims in that year. Many of them ended up in prison, among them, Mr. Izetbegovic himself. And they wanted to demonstrate to the Muslims the path they should follow, because he says the alienation of the Muslim people had instilled itself. It had become fairly prevalent, this alienation from their religion. It became a regular occurrence and the Muslims were in danger of losing their way in this secular society. And he says they imprisoned them, and I quote: "Over a thousand people went through the prisons and investigation process." And that all the prominent Muslims, in one way or another, were searched and investigated and taken through prisons or interrogations, interviews, and that this was a fate that all the former Young Muslims went through, those who were taken to court in previous years, 1946, 1947, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now let's move on to page 70, which in the Croatian text is 3D41-0252. And for the English it is on page 3D40-1565.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's just look at the end of that excerpt, where he says that the organisation was forcibly destroyed, but that it survived in the individuals, in the people. The organisation was destroyed, but people who believed in their ideas remained. And now I'd like to quote a sentence here, and I quote: "With them, memories and recollections survived, recollections of an organisation, its messages, demands and programme." And he says that a vast number of those people, the majority in fact, participated in the creation of the Party of Democratic Action in 1990. So there was no continuity, as far as the organisation itself was concerned, but there was continuity through people, through the human factor and their ideas and ideals, et cetera. So this was the oath that these people took; that they would work for the Muslims and for Islam. And these people throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina worked for the SDA. And then he goes on to say that from that aspect, we should assess the historical role of the Young Muslims organisation in those parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, on page 121, which is 3D41-0253 for the Croatian, and in English it is 3D40-1565, we have a text there which you wanted to comment on and show Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are documents which the author of this book quotes, the solemn oath by the Young Muslims. It's self-evident. And he goes on to say that they will adhere to all the regulations laid down in the Qur'an. And the important point here is that they will fight uncompromisingly against everything that is non-Islamic. Everything non-Islamic is hostile to Islam, according to the interpretation of the Young Muslims. And then he goes on to say that he will fight for the glory of Islam, for the well being of all Muslims throughout the world, for the greatness, power, and glory of Islam, as well as for the benefit of all the Muslims in the world, and that is the pan-Islamic movement, in their eyes. I'm not saying that. It's what they think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, on page 122, which is the same text in English, 3D40-1565 or, rather, 1566, and in Croatian 3D41-0254, we have something that you wish to highlight for Their Honours' benefit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a brochure or the copy of a brochure which was compiled for the purposes of the Young Muslims, and it talks about the fact that they must have -- or, rather, that they will be superior than their adversaries and foes; that they have ideological power and force and might, and that this provides them with the necessary superiority over their adversaries. And it goes on to say that this ideological strength will provide them with an iron will, and that they will have the necessary fanaticism and viciousness to protect and defend Islam, that they will be fanatics in a discussion, in the war of nerves, in polemics, and so on and so forth. Under point 2, he goes on to explain this -- or, rather, they go on to explain it. They say that in their collective, there must never be any discord and differences of opinion. And in point 3, he talks about the creation of an Islamic community and environment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're dealing with 3D40-1567 of the English version and 3D41-0255 for the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, they say that they will fight for the spiritual and material and the establishment of an Islamic order, the establishment of an Islamic culture and civilization, that that's what they will strive for. And then in point 5, there's a sentence there where they say: "Only once we have gained political power can we freely implement all the rules of Islam in an Islamic society." So political power is the basis for all this. It is a basis for them to be able to realise the premises of their movement, because then that will enable them to create a social system and a spiritual system according to their ideals propagated by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now we come to page 126. Yes, we can skip 24.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can skip 24 and go on to 126.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So page 126 is 3D41-0258 for the Croatian, and for the English it is 3D40-1568 and 3D40-1569.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a brochure, once again, written in Mostar and taken over in Sarajevo. Let me say that these brochures were written earlier on, not during this war, but they were written sometime after the Second World War. But they have remained and survived as a permanent oath and solemn declaration of that organisation. And it speaks of the shameful year of 1917, when the Serbs took control of the state after their victory in World War I, and how badly the Muslims fared, and so did the 21 Croats, they suffered too. And it says that to rely on the friendship between 22 the Serbs and Croats is the biggest nonsense and delusion of oneself and 23 one’s community, and that the Serbs and the Croats, it says, will never -- 24 well, they will never believe in their good intentions. And they refer to 25 the Qur’an again, which says, and I quote: "Shall ye seek friends among infidels." And once again I'm going to quote: "Neither Christians nor Jews will be your friends for as long as you refuse to accept what they stand for." And then it goes on -- they go on to explain what they mean -- what they think of the Serbs and the Croats, and it says that all they wish to do is to topple Islam and to take revenge for Kosovo, to loot and pilfer the crescent and so on. And then in the text, they go on to speak about pan-Islamism and the possibility of the practical application of Islam to life. And they say that with Allah's help, they will join the Jihad, and so on and so forth, right through to the end of the brochure. And I have nothing to add there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We shall now move to page 131, which is 3D41-0261 for the Croatian and 3D40-1570 for the English version.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another text which served as a set of instructions for the work of the members and the organisation on the ground. The instruction was drafted after the war, and I mean after the Second World War here. All the power wielders are here proclaimed infidels, under item 2 of this text. A reference is made to their distorted point of view, which has to be corrected. And it is also said that one has to be very fervent and adamant in attacking non-Islamic principles which are seen as good all over Europe and in the rest of the cultural world, and the "cultural" here is under the inverted commas, which means that that part of the world is seen as exactly the opposite, not being cultural. And here it says that the morale of that society is bad, that they're inhumane, that they speak against modern fine arts and sculpture, immoral works of literature, film. And it says here that Europe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It appears to Mr. Praljak that you now reading parts that are not in the translated document we have before us. Is that correct? Ms. Pinter, you can control.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should have been translated. However, I believe that we have a mistake in the last paragraph under number 2, and I will have an answer for you right away. We have translated all the pages that the general wanted to discuss. However, I'm lost among the pages at the moment. On page 3D41570, instead of the last paragraph under number 3, it should read the last paragraph under number 2, and you will be able to find the text -- the relevant text that the general has been quoting from, not the paragraph under 3 but rather the paragraph under 2.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the paragraph under number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: There is a mistake in the English translation, because it says here that the paragraph is under number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you please assist me by pointing to the reference on modern art and sculpture? That I have not yet found, and I might find my place again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 2, Nika, item 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 2. However, as regards modern arts -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the middle of item 2, modern art, sculpture, a big number of bad and immoral works of literature and films.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This hasn't been translated, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: How come? Very well then, if it hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That part has not been translated. Just one part has been translated, and herein lies the problem.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can skip that. It goes on here to say that America and Europe are founded on very bad and rotten foundations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is the end of that, and I would like to ask you just one more question now that we've been through the topic or, rather, the book, "The Young Muslims." What is in this book that you have considered important for the Trial Chamber? What is important for the understanding of the context of the indictment and the events that ensued?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Mr. Izetbegovic said, the idea remained in the heads of the thousands of people who belonged to the organisation which promoted this, and those people later on took over the SDA completely. Of course, one cannot assume that people who fought for decades for that idea of theirs, that they changed all of a sudden, that they changed their school of thought. One has to understand this kind of thoughts that existed among a number of people in order to understand everything that happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because those people were in charge of the party. If you don't understand this, you will not be able to understand why a lot of effort that we invested, we Croats, either in Croatia or in the HZ-HB, why all the negotiations and cease-fires fell through, why nothing came out of our strives to create a joint command, why all this failed, and why, for that matter, the Mujahedin were so well received and they had such a strong support in Central Bosnia. You will not understand all that if you don't know what the background of all of that was, the ideological background. I believe that this is all very important for the understanding of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I would kindly ask you now to take document 3D00855 --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We have to discuss the end of item 3 or, rather, 2, which has been translated. The end of item 2 has been translated. I can see that. It says here that one has to be on a standby and fully prepared, that they have to demonstrate the fervour and the sincere desire to destroy everything that is non-Islamic. So the essence of the movement among these people, of course I'm not going to talk about all Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina of whom I know that a majority of them were not infested or not accepted these ideas; however, the nucleus of this organisation treated everything non-Islamic in the same way the Serbs treated everything that was non-Serb. And this is the essence for the understanding of any future events that ensued. And then we have just one small part in item 3, which is on page 132.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is 3D40-1570 and 1571 for the English version, and 3D41-0262 for the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just that little portion. They point to the fact that in discussions, their goals have to be pointed out, and their goals are to create and education real Muslims who will be the custodians of Islam on the Balkans, and that was the most important task at that moment, and also the unity of the Islamic world, with a view of creating the possibility for the implementation of the laws of Qur'an and Hadis, which means that the state organisation has to be established in accordance with the Qur'an and not vice versa. And then on page 133, items 3, 4, and 5, I want to go through them just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D41-0263, and in the English it is 3D40-1571.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here you have a list of everything that is banned. There is a ban on visiting mixed beaches and promenades. There's a ban on dancing. And it says that a Muslim who would engage in all that would not be a good Muslim; he would not be on the Jihad road. And if they do not behave in the way they should, they would be eradicated by the rest of Europe. They have to put up against and remain victorious, and that's why no entertainment may be allowed. And it goes on to say under item 5 that they shouldn't go to the theaters, operas, ballet performances, circuses, cinemas. All that is -- and then on the following page 134 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D41-0264, and 3D40-1571 for the English version.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then he goes on to explain that the theatre is based on acting, and this is enough for the theatre to be rejected, rejected by everybody. It says that Europe has more harm than benefit from the theatre that they foster. It says that men and women come into contact as actors and behind the scenes in the theatre, and this should be banned and rejected. In other words, an actor cannot be a wife and a mother, as they should be, and so on and so forth. And then under item 7, it says that hand -- shaking women's hands should be minimised, because this is not in accordance with Islam. You shouldn't be the one to shake -- to extend your hand to shake a woman's hand first. If you do that -- if you don't extend your hand, the women will understand that you don't want to shake hands with her, and that will serve to avoid any non-Islamic way of communication. So this would be all from the book that I wanted to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you to go to 3D00855. The book is in binder 3, for the Trial Chamber, and in the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you said something earlier, but it's not on the screen anymore. But you said that according to you, when reading the book, according to you the state must be organised along the Qur'an, and it shouldn't be the other way around. So you said this, and I looked at the text to see if this had been written black on white, and I can't see it. I can't see it black on white. So is this a conclusion that you're drawing from this, that you're inferring? Or was this actually said in Mr. Izetbegovic's interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the rules that I was reading from, it is spelled out explicitly. I can find it for you, if you will allow me to do so. I've even quoted from that part. It says here that in order to implement the Qur'an, society has to be fully Islamised. It doesn't say so explicitly in Mr. Izetbegovic's interview, but it does say so very explicitly in the rules from which I was reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 15 -- Senka, once again, please. 3D41-151040.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance. I apologise for standing up. It's easier than communicating with my learned friend sitting down. I can see that Mr. Praljak had in front of him page 3D40-1570 when he was discussing this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the instructions for work, page 131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But, General Praljak, let me ask you one thing. The fact that Mr. Izetbegovic, Young Muslims, are saying that everything must be Islamised, does it mean that he believes everyone must be a Muslim and everybody must have a Koran, without this leading to ethical, legal, or state modifications? Do you believe that this leads immediately to changes in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina? That is the crux of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct, Your Honours, that this would mean a fundamental change in the constitution. However, this is just the road that they want to take. They want to implement the project. They want to realise the project. Some people were obviously aware that at that moment that was not really possible, and that is why, in the Islamic Declaration that I personally -- since it was printed in so many copies and everybody read it, it says there, We are not in a position to do this right now; however, if we end up having Bosnia and Herzegovina the way we want it to be, then Mr. Izetbegovic says explicitly, When we have 51 percent, then we will have a possibility, since we will have a majority, to choose the government that will change the constitution. And then we will be able to create a constitution which will befit the Islamic religious teaching.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, let us go back to the initial document that I've already mentioned, 3D00855. That's a book entitled "The Time of the Infidel." It was written by Mr. Tudjman, and just to say that this was also in the same packet where the book "The Young Muslims" were. General, you wanted this book to be presented to the Court, and could you please tell us at the outset why you think it's important for the Court to be aware of the facts from this book?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because in the course of the proceedings, there were several occasions where a secret meeting between Milosevic and Tudjman was mentioned, the meeting in Karadjordjevo, which being a secret meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. The transcript indicates that the title of the book is called "The Time of the Infidel." What I have is "A Time of Perjury," and I just wanted to clarify that we're all with the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter agrees, it is "The Time of Perjury --" perjurer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the same exhibit, and the transcript just did not reflect it correctly. So it is "The Time of the Perjurer."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, please go on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this mythology and in this whole story of, what I would call, something that came from the spin doctor's laboratory about the facts of the war of 1991 to 1995, I refer to these people as Ostap Bender characters. And these people are like those from the Ostap Bender workshop to produce Ostap Bender characters which produced lies. However, because they were so professional in producing lies, and according to the old Goebbels precepts, they always perpetuated -- always perpetuating anew the story, until those people who do not really deal with the problem finally begin to belief in it, and it becomes a fact, so the perception of this lie becomes a fact. In other words, it becomes the truth. One such lie that had its ramifications in all these states was that Milosevic and Tudjman, in 1991, held a secret meeting in Karadjordjevo where they agreed on the division of Bosnia. Your Honours, I spoke on several occasions about this being logical lunacy, because if Milosevic did have the plans that he did, and he was attacking in order to implement those plans, how would then they divide Bosnia? But who cares about logics. After all the stories that were circulating, this story was totally of no interest, in the political sense. And for this same reason, the son of Franjo Tudjman, Miroslav Tudjman, who was, by the way, an acquaintance since 1971, and he is a professor of Communications, a university professor, and he's well aware how information can be manipulated and how it is produced, he wrote this book to, as he says, defend the truth, but also, in part, to defend his father. And I would just like to point out some portions of that book - not too many - in order to show how it really was and what it was all about. And this is why I feel that this Court should see some of those portions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, does this book contain the positions of the author, in other words, Miroslav Tudjman, or just the facts that you want to refer to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to refer to the facts. His positions are completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since you mentioned the secret meeting in Karadjordjevo, we can go to page 136 in Croatian. That is 3D23-0407, and in English this would be 3D23-0761. And then it goes on to the next page, 3D23-0762 and 3D23-0763. General, please go on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here we can see Mr. Miroslav Tudjman, first of all, denies this tenet that this was a secret meeting, and he mentions the research conducted by Dusan Bilandzic, an academic, who testified in this Tribunal, in the Blaskic case, where the Prosecutor Kehoe mentioned the secret meeting, but he couldn't even recall the date of this meeting, whether it was on the 10th or the 11th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects to this exhibit. Mr. President, I've been looking at the table of contents. It appears to be Mr. Tudjman's comments on trial proceedings in the Blaskic case, the Blaskic judgement. He's certainly entitled to his opinion on that, but it seems to me that his opinions aren't really any more legitimate than anyone else's. And commenting on proceedings in another trial isn't going to really be of any relevant use to the Trial Chamber. That's all this is, and we object to this. It's wasting our time. I suggest we move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you believe it's a waste of time, and the Defence believes that it's not. The Judges do not have all the elements at hand to know anything. You know, they read the Blaskic judgement and the trial, as everyone else. I know that in this document there is mention of Mr. Kehoe, the Prosecutor who was during the examination-in-chief, and if I'm not mistaken, now Mr. Kehoe is the Defence counsel of Mr. Gotovina, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add something, Your Honour. I've explicitly asked the general if the positions of the author will be put forth or just the facts alone. Now, we will not discuss the entire book, but only the facts that are relevant for this assessment, whether a secret meeting was actually held in Karadjordjevo, and this is in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll hold my fire, if I may put it that way. Maybe just one brief remark, if I can make it in private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on this page that we have before us, HINA, the news agency, Croatian news agency, as all countries have these agencies, this agency is called HINA. So on the 25th of March HINA published that Milosevic and Tudjman met -- had met in Karadjordjevo and that they discussed the economic crisis, the future relations within Yugoslavia, the forthcoming meetings of republican presidents, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, will you tell us what year this was.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991. Next, now this on page 48 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In English, that's 3D23-0764 and 3D23-0765; and in Croatian that's 3D23-0408.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here, further on it says they concluded that in order to resolve the current Yugoslav problems, two months should be foreseen for this resolution; that the Chamber of Commerce of Yugoslavia's proposal for the change the federal government should be discussed, and this was what this meeting was about. Further on, in a Ljubljana paper and Radio Slovenia, and this again was reported by HINA on the 26th of March, so the Slovenia media also reported on this meeting, and they state that this policy between Tudjman and Milosevic, which was contradictory in itself, was beginning to affect Milosevic's position, and also the authority that Tudjman had. And in Belgrade there were already mass rallies against Milosevic. In Knin, the Knin Krajina was already threatening to secede. And of course all of this put Tudjman in a completely different situation, facing a different problem, how to resolve that. And again a period of two months is mentioned. And then there is also talk about the removal of Ante Markovic, who was at the time the prime minister, the president of the Federal Executive Council. And it says that many issues were touched upon which still await resolution. And, of course, this is what the Slovenian journalists were able to learn. Next, HINA, on the 27th of March, quotes the reporting in the French Catholic newspaper, "La Croix," where it says that Yugoslavia was on the way to confederalism, something along the lines of the European community, and they published the well-known analysis of the historian -- now, I'm not sure how I'm going to read this in French -- Francois Feuilleteau, where he says that this meeting was a great step forward in the restructuring of Yugoslavia. And then the German Handelsblatt also speaks -- reports on this meeting. The report is by Georg von Hubbenet, the Belgrade correspondent of that newspaper, stating that the formal constitutional amendments should be in place and whether -- and so on and so forth. And then there is also mention whether to accept the proposal by the Chamber of Commerce, and so on and so forth. In other words, here at this time there's still discussion about confederation, so Tudjman was still hopeful that he would be able to talk Milosevic into abandoning his rigid political plan. Of course, that was an illusion, but he was making an effort. And then further on it says that they adopted a conclusion which is here toward the end of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just to say in English, this is 3D23-0766 in English, and in Croatian it's still the same page.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they agreed that presidents of republics will meet to find the solution. This was the period when there were rotational meetings of presidents of each republic. They would move from one to the other republic. They met if Sarajevo, Zagreb, Belgrade, Skopje. They travelled from place to place as a group of men who were trying to resolve this Gordian knot. However, the political options that Milosevic had, and all the others, they were not possible to bridge, the gap that existed between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D23-0409 is the number for the Croatian, and for the English it is 3D23-0767 and 0768 and 69.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, and we've already seen this in this trial, I presented a letter written by Mr. Izetbegovic to Franjo Tudjman in his own hand, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment, General. That is Exhibit 3D00295. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyway, from this letter we can see that Alija had already heard from some of these spin doctors and agents about the story. The story was already going 'round put out by them that Milosevic would offer up a division of Bosnia and Herzegovina to Franjo Tudjman before the meeting actually took place. So the meeting hadn't even taken place and rumours were already going 'round as to what was being offered up, and all with the aim of preventing a possible better alliance between the Croats and Muslims. So that was very simple; it was a very simple thing. And on page 141, one can conclude what we were going -- what we see later on when Milosevic says it, and he says, For goodness sake, had there been an agreement on the carve-up of Bosnia, we wouldn't have needed any of the following meetings and the war wouldn't have gone the way it went, because when Milosevic's power, with the Yugoslav People's Army behind him, had he reached an agreement with Franjo Tudjman on the division of Bosnia, then Bosnia would have been carved up within the space of five days. So that's it, and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Page 144 in the book is page 3D23-0411 on e-court for the Croatian, and in English it is 3D23-0774 and 3D23-0775, and on what's 3D-0776. Go ahead, please, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time -- well, since meetings were being held, this story about Karadjordjevo no longer existed, but it was brought up again in 1993. There was a resurgence when, for some dark forces, they wanted to revive the Muslim-Croat conflict and disputes. And then the Muslims were told once again, Well, there you go, Franjo Tudjman divided up Bosnia and shared it up with Milosevic a long time ago. So that was the reason why this problem, which from 1991 to 1993 didn't crop up, suddenly re-emerged in 1993, and stories were going 'round about some division two years previously. In the meantime, the war had flared up and so on. And so mention is made here of the letter of the 16th of July, 1993, which was sent by Franjo Tudjman to the Secretary-General of the United Nations, Boutros Boutros-Ghali from VONS, and he says that the pressure and claims made that Croatia was concerned, and he says that Croatia recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as an integral and sovereign country, whereas there 25 had been no agreement between Croatia -- well, anyway – and Serbia - about 1 the division of Bosnia. Croatia was cooperative in seeking a solution, 2 Croatia would support any solution acceptable to the peoples of Bosnia- 3 Herzegovina, and so on and so forth. Croatia supports the principle of 4 territorial integrity and independence and autonomy, and that the war could 5 end and so on. Unfortunately, Mr. Tudjman had to justify himself, because the perception was -- that was going 'round was that there had been a division in 1991, and now they're using it as a fact. So we all found the need to justify ourselves from these fabrications that were going 'round. And furthermore, Tudjman goes on to say -- well, he kept repeating to the journalists, and he says here again, I repeat, once and for all, that never was there any alleged agreement on the division of Bosnia between myself and the other side. And that is to be found in footnote 31, and everything is explained there, the agreements that had been signed and so on. And in part F, and I can testify to this myself -- well, in all the negotiations and talks, Your Honours, Croatia always requested that UNPROFOR should not only stand between the two parties in Croatia, the two sides in Croatia, that is to say Milan Martic's forces and Milan Babic's one side in Croatia, but to take positions along the borders of Croatia. So if Croatia was a recognised state and we kept repeating this, then take up positions along the Croatian borders, so to stop the war from spilling over. However, that never happened, once again, for reasons that are not quite clear, because from the very beginning of the war, when emissaries were sent to the territory, the international forces, all they had to do was to deploy along the borders of Croatia and -- Serbia and Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and nobody would be able to touch them, and then states within those borders could be -- lay down conditions, and they could state that minorities had to be protected, that the constitutions and laws must be along the lines of those in Europe. So what I'm saying is that the war could have been prevented very easily at the very beginning, had there been the will to do so. Now, let's stay on that page, and here Milosevic said -- told this to Ms. Zilber [phoen] and Alan Little in 1996 on the books they wrote, on page 124 of that book. And Milosevic says, Tudjman told me that he wants an independent state. We couldn't agree on that. That is to say, Milosevic could not agree to that. And he says there was speculation about the fact that we had agreed to carve up Yugoslavia. And he was always direct in his speech, and he says this very directly, and he says, I'm telling you now, had we decided to do so there, we could have done it straight away. Had we decided to do so there, we could have done it. And that's the crux of the matter. Had the strong Serb forces reached an agreement with Croatia, which also had its own forces, on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who could have stood up to that? They could have put it into practice in the space of three days. And he says, We could have done it straight away, and he wouldn't have attacked Croatia immediately afterwards, and we wouldn't have had the events that followed in 1995. And then further on, on page 146 and 147 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Those are pages 3D23-0412 for the Croatian, and 3D23-0777 for the English, on to 0778 and 0779.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have a quotation -- a statement made by President Tudjman to Milosevic from Geneva on the 17th of July, 1993, something they both signed, a statement that was signed by both of them. And they state that speculations about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina between Serbia and Croatia are completely unfounded. And, secondly, they agree that for lasting peace to be achieved in Bosnia-Herzegovina, an assertion of the interests of all three constituent peoples must be met and agreement reached on the establishment of three republics within the frameworks of a confederation. So those were the proposals made by Stoltenberg and Lord Owen at the time, that was their plan. So they say that they agreed to the plan, and speak of this solution, and go on to say that -- well, Borislav Jovic states his views on that later on, and he was Milosevic's right-hand man. They did everything but sleep together, I think. Anyway, he says, Well, as far as I'm concerned, that would have been a great surprise to me, because at that point in time a solution of that kind would have meant a deviation from our overall policy. So Jovic says that our overall policy was not to gain a part of Bosnia but to gain a Yugoslavia up to Karlobag, Virovitica, and Karlovac, up to those borders. And then Jovic speaks up again, and this is recorded in the footnote. He says that Milosevic hid this from him -- or, rather, he said that this wasn't possible because it wasn't in keeping with the goals of the Serb leadership, and it would be in contravention with our views of the way in which the Serb question should be solved in Croatia, and with our concept of preserving Yugoslavia. So that's quite clear. It was Serbia's policy to resolve the Serb issue in Croatia in the way in which we have seen, and all the books and articles written about this say how this was to be done. And Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to that plan, including three-quarters of Croatia, was to be incorporated into Yugoslavia. On pages 148 and 149, well, Professor Smilja Abramov, who took part in this, says the same thing. She addresses that issue, so there's no need for us to go into that. Bilandzic says the same thing, that there were no talks, no meeting. Milan Babic does the same, and Milosevic promised him a state on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that's what that deals with. But we can move on, if you want briefly to look at the final section.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That is on page 3D23-0437, and it's page 197 of the book. In English, it is 3D23-0847 onwards. We're not going to skip any pages, so I don't have to quote the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Before you address this document: From what I understand, when I listen to you, I believe that you challenge that this secret meeting ever took place, when this secret meeting is something which was noted as a fact in the Blaskic judgement, in paragraph 105 of the judgement. You challenge this version of the facts. That's all very well, but maybe this is something which you're going to discuss later. Milosevic, who was tried here, must have been questioned about this meeting. Did you look into this and see what he may have said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say with certainty, but I think that he said at this trial -- at that trial as well, first of all, the meeting wasn't a secret one because it was broadcast by the media, so how could it be secret if the Germans and French and Croats and everybody else writes about it? And, secondly, everybody took part, Abramov, Bilandzic, Babic, Milosevic, Tudjman, and all of them say -- well, never mind the fact that they say this, but logically, logically, if you look at it logically, Milosevic couldn't have had a political plan to have a Yugoslavia of this type and then to divide up Bosnia-Herzegovina with this man. That goes against the grain. It is illogical, because you exclude two options in one head. And I think that Milosevic confirms that here in talking to a witness. I think that Stipo Mesic was a witness, and I think he took this up with him, although I can't say for certain. So I'm challenging -- or, rather, the documents are challenging -- well, the meeting was held. The meeting was not secret, and there was not, nor could there have been with these political options on the table, could there have been any talk of the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the meeting. And had that happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. I was of the opinion that we were hearing a witness. I hear pleading after pleading, discussions of opinions of others they write in book, the others quote others again, and the others again are quoted by the Court again. In my view, Mr. Praljak, I'm sorry, this is not testimony. This is not talking about facts. This is sheer pleading. And the pleading, of course, is something legitimate, but this is not the moment for it. And would really think that it would be conducive to the good conduct of these proceedings if we can find our way back to what can truly be called testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Mr. Praljak, my colleague is drawing your attention to this fact. We need to know whether this meeting actually took place or not. You have said that this meeting took place, but at the meeting the carving up of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not addressed, as the Prosecutor ascertains. Now, to prove this fact, it is necessary, on the basis of documents which are shown to you, to tell us that the meeting was organised for another reason, other than the reason put forward by the Prosecutor. That is a fact we're interested in. Have you understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the meeting was held, Your Honour. It wasn't secret, because the Slovenes were reporting on it, as well as the Croatian agency, and the French journals, German newspapers, and so on. And according to the information at that time, they stated what was discussed at the meeting. Never at that time was any mention made of the fact that at that meeting there was an agreement on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I took part at the time in the political life, if I can put it that way, of the country, and nowhere did you have mention of the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The division of Bosnia-Herzegovina began to appear at the meeting in 19 -- or, rather, began to be written about in 1993, and I quoted Tudjman's letter, Boutros-Ghali's statement, Milosevic's statement. I said what Borislav Jovic thought about the matter, and all the other people taking part, and they all said that that just did not happen. So what evidence do you want me to present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the Chamber seized of the Blaskic case -- well, since you have mentioned this, I have mentioned the Blaskic judgement. And in that judgement it is stated that this confidential meeting was held. There are four footnotes which I don't see right now. I shall read the judgement a little later on, and I would like to see what these footnotes refer to. 204, 205, 206, and 207, these are the footnotes. And it seems that it's on the basis of these four footnotes that the Chamber draws its conclusion. They may have made a mistake; I don't know. But as far as you are concerned, without pleading here the facts, you are saying that this meeting was not organised for the reasons that some people claim it was organised for; am I right in saying this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. The story about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina appeared only in 1993. You saw yesterday, Your Honours, that at the same time when this notorious meeting was taking place, Filipovic was talking to Tudjman and Tudjman was offering things for Bosnia and Herzegovina which were totally different, and this was simultaneous. The arrival of Mr. Filipovic in Zagreb and Slovenia that we discussed yesterday coincided with this alleged division of Bosnia and Herzegovina by Franjo Tudjman and the others. I claim, based on everything I know, on the facts that I'm aware of, that the meeting was not secret, and there's no single participant that will assert that it dealt with the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That political lie appeared only in 1993 in order to put pressure on Croatia and only for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me, I would like to point to an ambiguity in the interpretation that might lead to a misunderstanding. On page 30, lines 17 and 18, and page 31, line 11, if I -- it says that the stories on the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina appeared only in 1993. If I understood General Praljak properly, he said that in 1993, stories appeared about the meeting in Karadjordjevo discussing the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, my learned friend Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, at the Karadjordjevo meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Just to finish talking about this subject, you mentioned Mr. Mesic, and I see that in Miroslav Tudjman's book, he mentions this. Now, to sum up, what did Mr. Mesic say about this meeting held in Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mesic testified at this Tribunal, and he said that he had heard that at that meeting Bosnia-Herzegovina was being carved up. This book was written about that testimony. Stipe Mesic perjured himself, and he was telling lies here, 4 and he did that because he wanted to settle political scores with Franjo 5 Tudjman, both alive or dead, actually more dead than alive. This was after 6 Franjo Tudjman’s death. Mr. Mesic did not present truthful facts. Mr. Mesic, 7 as you could see in "The Croatian Soldier," "Hrvatski Vojnik," in 1993, in 8 his interview, he says that their policies that they were pursuing was wise. 9 Now, the question arises: How come Mr. Mesic, in 1991, if he heard that the 10 division of Bosnia and Herzegovina was discussed by Tudjman and Milosevic, 11 that he was against, why didn't he say so publicly and openly at that time? 12 And he was the second person in the state, just next to Franjo Tudjman. How 13 come that he never mentioned that in any of the meetings, some of which I 14 attended? He was waiting for everything to pass, and only then did he engage 15 in settling political scores with a dead man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm going to object to this 17 speculation on the part of the general. He can give his own theories and 18 suppositions as to why he thinks someone else did or didn't do anything, 19 but it's not relevant evidence. The question was: What did Mesic say? 20 And that has now become a speech against words and testimony of another 21 witness in this Tribunal. Ultimately, it's for the Trial Chamber to 22 decide. But it's my objection that this sort of comments and criticism, 23 coming from an accused who's in the box, is not helpful and it's not 24 relevant. If he could just address himself to the question that came 25 from the Trial Chamber, which was: What did Mesic say about Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that General Praljak was answering questions and that he said it loud and clear as to how Stipo Mesic reacted, and he shared with us only the facts. He said that Stipo Mesic, from 1991, was involved in politics, and that in 1991, if he had been aware of this so-called secret meeting and the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina discussed at that meeting, he never said anything about that in 1991. So the general is not presenting his views and his assessments. He is presenting only the facts which were taking place, and in doing that he quoted from "Hrvatski Vojnik," which was discussed here, in which Stipo Mesic never pointed to the fact that the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been discussed or agreed between Tudjman and Milosevic. I believe, therefore, that General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Pinter. I find it difficult to accept that Mr. Praljak is talking about facts. He's reading from books. He's reading from books and saying what other people think happened. That, I'm sorry, is not facts. That is opinions of other people. I'm very sorry. If he were present at some time, if he could say, I have heard Mr. Tudjman say this, that would be different. The fact that he lived at that time doesn't make him a witness of these things. And he does not say, I know this and that. He reads from books. This is not testimony. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Please bear with me. Your Honours, the facts are as follows: In 1991, 1992, 1993, I was a member of the VONS, and I met with Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Mesic at many meetings. Never, ever, not for a single moment, not with a single word, did anybody mention, and that includes Mr. Mesic, any story regarding the fact that Franjo Tudjman and Milosevic, in 1991, in the spring of that year, had agreed on the division of Bosnia. That story, and this is my experience which I am testifying to, appeared only in 1993, two years subsequently, two years after the meeting. And I know that the story turned up out of the blue because the political show-downs had started. I know that. Stipo Mesic was not at that meeting. He knows all I know. He testified about that meeting here, and he also speculated. There were two people at the meeting, and those people said what they had to say. And what I'm saying now is my testimony, and the facts are listed in here. They have been publicised, and this is my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, what you have told us now was, in fact, your testimony, and that's fine. I have no problem with your saying, I have never heard anything of that kind. That is your testimony. But then what so many other people told third people, that goes beyond what is testimony. It's expertise, perhaps, a history lesson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just add one thing, Your Honours. Your Honours, we are here presenting our case, the Defence case. It is not up to us to prove anything. We don't have the burden of proof. The Prosecution included this thesis on the secret meeting in Karadjordjevo in the indictment, and they offered some evidence which was nothing but hearsay in the second or third instance. And their evidence boiled down to, This gentleman heard that or that gentleman heard something else. In his testimony, Mr. Praljak has found some facts that he is testifying to, and finally he has just told us what he knows directly. And he can only say what other people are saying, and especially what the participants were saying, or very close associates of the participants, and that's what we have just heard. And I believe that this is just the kind of testimony which is necessary about the facts that exist in the reality that the Defence and the accused have managed to find or organise, and that includes also the part, but is also that part that the accused is personally aware of. This is his direct, personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I'll check something with you and then we'll take a break, so I'll be very short. You told us that you were a member of the VONS, that you attended the meetings of the VONS, which is the supreme organ with the Presidency of Croatia, in 1991, 1992, and 1993. We have a number of minutes of these meetings. I don't know, but I'll check whether we have any minutes from 1991. But you attended these meetings, so please tell us the following: When Mr. Tudjman met foreign political dignitaries, did he necessarily during this meeting tell all the attendants, who were not very numerous -- did he tell what the members of the VONS, who were not very numerous, what had been addressed during these meetings with foreigners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honours, save for the VONS meetings, there was a series of other meetings which were not official, with Tudjman, Mesic and others. At those meetings, we discussed hundreds of matters. Second of all, Your Honours, up to 1993 I never heard anybody mentioning the secret meeting in Karadjordjevo and the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Third of all, Your Honours, Franjo Tudjman, and I know that for a fact, this is my testimony, Franjo Tudjman had a shortcoming when discussing things with people, that people misunderstood very often, especially Americans. He tried to separate his own pragmatic political position. He tried to show cooperativeness, democracy, and all the things that we discussed, but he also wanted to show these people, and that was his mistake, he wanted to explain to everybody the historical context, and all those people did not have the time for that, especially Americans didn't have the time to listen to all that. The Americans would come, they would have 15 minutes in order to deal with the problem of the states, just like they do with the problems of the Wall Street investment and so on and so forth. And that kind of approach bothered them; they didn't understand that. And if they did understand something, they misunderstood things, and they thought erroneously and often what their talks boiled down to was nothing but a misunderstanding. They thought his historical interpretations were tantamount to his political views. And let me conclude, Your Honours, I, myself, tried to explain there to my president. I tried to explain to him that those people did not have the desire or goodwill to listen to everything, to everything about the historical forces that were trying to get involved in the war and that he felt as a historian. I tried to tell him to opt for shorter and pragmatical solutions, but it fell on deaf ears. This was the source of a misunderstanding that I tried to point out to my president as the cause of the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just put one more question before the break, before the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we'll have the break. We're already late. So you'll come back to this after the break. We have everything in mind, and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, I believe you had a question that you wanted to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. The question had to do with your question; namely, I assess that General Praljak had not fully answered your question, so I wanted to point it out to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: A portion of the question of Judge Antonetti was whether at VONS President Tudjman informed you on his meetings with foreign representatives.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand that part of the question. Otherwise, I would have answered it. My answer is yes, yes, and we will here present some minutes of those meetings. Not only did he inform us of that; that was one of the main things that President Tudjman was involved in, and that was he wanted to try and understand what the countries of the international community actually wanted to see happen there, and then he wanted to try and find some sort of position that would be acceptable for his policies so that he would be able to establish Croatia, because there were many representatives of various countries that had different positions. The international community, and we could see this from the documents, that France, Germany, Britain, America, they did not have a single position. Each country had their own view, and it was very difficult to understand what was the plan for each of those actors for the Balkans, and that was one of the things that President Tudjman had as his preoccupation. He wanted to adapt to the international situation because he was aware that without being adapted and without actually winning over the West so that they could understand what it was that he was after, he would not be able to create Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, earlier you talked about Witness Bilandzic. Who exactly is this person? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bilandzic was -- he is a historian. Actually, he was a Communist historian, to be honest. His "ouvre" that I've read in good part, I consider that it was completely partial. But, in any case, the party also promoted him into academician, although he was not very active in the political events, President Tudjman actually asked him to take a role on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had never heard of this person, but he's mentioned in the Blaskic judgement. It's a public judgement, and I believe that I can refer to it. This historian, published a paper in "Nacional" in October 1996, and it was about this negotiation. And he would have -- that's in judgement that two commissions would have been set up, two commissions that had been organized to discuss how Bosnia-Herzegovina was to be divided. In the Blaskic judgement, to say it all, the Trial Chamber continues and says -- it links the Babic-Karadzic meeting in Graz, with this one, so it seems that there is a logic. Now, to your knowledge, can you tell us whether commissions were actually set up to discuss the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the Blaskic Trial Chamber seems to be indicating it in its judgement on paragraph 205? I had to do some research during the break. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Bilandzic, in his text which was published in "Nacional," I can say, and that would be putting it mildly, he's not speaking the truth. And in the Blaskic case, on page 150 of this book, a quotation was taken out, and Ms. Nika can find it for you, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's in English 3D23-0783 and 3D23-0784 and 85, whereas in Croatian that would be 3D23-0414.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and even before this, Ms. Abramov referred to that. But here we can see that he speaks of some sort of commission where discussions were, for the most part -- 95 percent of the discussions related to the 1974 constitution. And then it says as for maps and some specific divisions, that was not under discussion. We did not discuss at all the carving up of the borders between Serbia and Croatia in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because my colleagues and I did not believe at all in the realism of such a policy, and we thought that we shouldn't enter into it at all. Now, if Franjo Tudjman established a committee that was to carve up Bosnia and Herzegovina, why would he then discuss whether it should be carved up or not? And this was not something that they discussed. Now, the committee on the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would appear from this, was something that Franjo Tudjman had come up with, but these are subsequent political games being played, and this is in retaliation by a Communist historian who did not agree with Tudjman. And here we can see what Blaskic said; that there were no borders drawn up. He had the role, and had he been given a task to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina, he could have refused to implement it, but he did not get such a task. They were discussing the constitution, and most of the time was devoted to that. And on the previous page, 148, Dr. Smilja Abramov speaks about this. She was a Serbian president of the Constitutional Court, and we can see here what Ms. Abramov said about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for your information, and also in part as an answer to the honourable Judge Trechsel, the Defence dealt with this topic also because this honourable Chamber, on the 7th of September, 2006, established the decision on adjudicated facts, one of them being paragraph 105 from the Blaskic judgement, which deals with the meeting between Dr. Tudjman and Milosevic and the division or partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the Defence has the right to question those facts, the adjudicated facts, and that's one of the reasons why we are discussing this now and why we are referring to the facts that we have at our disposal, just as they were at the disposal of those who had discussed them in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction: Agreed facts, not adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just have to make it quite clear that I do not in any way challenge your right to contest whatever you want to contest. That was not my point. My point was more a technical one of what can be regarded as testimony, as opposed to, for instance, contesting and arguing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can testify to two things. First, all these meetings that were held up until 1993, in all those meetings I had never heard that there was any mention of the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Karadjordjevo. I did not hear it from Dr. Franjo Tudjman, Mr. President. I didn't hear it from the president -- or the speaker of Parliament, Mr. Mesic. I didn't hear it from any of the chiefs of -- from the chief of all the security services and intelligence services of Croatia. I didn't hear it from Gojko Susak or from the prime minister, the president of the Croatian government, Mr. Gligoric. No one ever mentioned that, none of them. That's number 1. Number 2, and I've said this before, there is a major misunderstanding between the internal governance of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was always referred to as the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In other words, the Cutileiro plan was referred to as the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina both in "Javnost" and in other papers. The Vance-Owen Plan was also referred to as the partition or division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Owen-Stoltenberg Plan was also referred to as the division or partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I know that President Tudjman -- Presidents Tudjman, Izetbegovic, and Milosevic met on the 12th of April in Split, in the Dalmacija Villa. This was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the date, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if this information is accurate, but that was about that time, anyway. They met, and this meeting lasted for five hours, which was followed by a press communique. But it was leaked to the press that there was this meeting, and here is what the papers published about the meeting of these three presidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I won't read this from the article, because I know of this myself. This is my testimony. So it was leaked that at this time, they had also discussed the internal governance or type of government for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the papers published this under the following titles: "Vecernji List," "Bosnia, like Switzerland." This was on the 13th of June, 1991. Then the next title was "The Collapse of Yugoslavia." Then the following title, "Cantonisation of Interest." And then "Slobodna Dalmacija" published "Cantons, A Done Deal?" And then "Oslobodjenje" publishes this "There Will be no partition." And then the "Danas Weekly" from Croatia published an article under the title of "All Bosnian Nuances." And then in "Oslobodjenje", we see "The Cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, For and Against Nebulous Ideas." And then in "Vijesti," a daily from Croatia, we see an article entitled, "Cantonisation is Impossible." "Borba," the Serbian daily, says "How Many Cantons for the Land of Bosnia." And so on and so forth. So I've already said this before. This concept of the internal government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was repeatedly referred to as the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this is the reason why then this was translated into an understanding that this was an agreement between Serbia and Croatia on the partition of Bosnia. And what I can say is that until 1993, never was any mention made by anyone of the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina in any of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday or the day before, you were able to see what the -- what President Tudjman knew when he explained to Mr. Filipovic what was going to happen, and that came before this particular meeting. So compare the two. Compare what President Tudjman told Filipovic, and his knowledge about how events would develop, and the testimony of Mr. Mesic. That's my first point. Secondly, why is Mr. Mesic saying that at a meeting of the Croatian Assembly or VONS, and nowhere up to 1993, or I don't know when, when he separated from President Tudjman -- when was that, you say? When was it? 1994, is that what you say? It was only when he -- when each of them went their different political ways that he began telling this story. And the "Hrvatski Vojnik" is a paper that I helped edit. In the interview that I showed you, Mesic says, Let's wage a reasonable policy from 1993. So wouldn't it then be logical that after this information from President Tudjman, he didn't say, Mr. President, I don't agree with that, and present his views, say that out loud? No, Your Honours. No, no, and again no. The facts brought out here about the meeting was within a settling of accounts, political settling of accounts, and has nothing to do with what happened and what I'm testifying about here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The general referred to the talk between Dr. Tudjman and Muhamed Filipovic from document 3D03554. The page in the Croatian is 3D41-0834. And for the record, on page 42, line 8, the name of the individual you mentioned was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Who was the head of all the secret and intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Manolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Josip Manolic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, yes, in Croatia, I meant. Now, General, in your book -- or, rather, we referred to the letter written by Alija Izetbegovic to President Tudjman, and that is 3D00295, and it's already an exhibit in this trial. But, anyway, Alija Izetbegovic knew that a meeting would be held. Now, do you know whether Dr. Tudjman and Milosevic informed Alija Izetbegovic about that meeting which they held in Karadjordjevo and whether there was any discussion about the meeting, since that was a time when the presidents were meeting and circulating, had these rotational meetings, as you said earlier on today? If you know about that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Izetbegovic knew that a meeting would be held. He was in contact with President Tudjman, and I do believe that he was informed about it. But the essential point here is that somebody already, as Franjo Tudjman says, one of those KOS people or State Security people, that somebody had already put forward the thesis according to which Milosevic is going to put a document on the table to Franjo to divide up -- to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, after some ten meetings that were held, it became obvious what was afoot, so that here this false -- this red herring is being put forward, and that's something that Tudjman says to Filipovic. He says, Let's move together, but Izetbegovic, as he says, under the influence of these other people, and he said, It will be difficult to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let's move now to page 197 and look at the 48 meetings between President Tudjman and Milosevic, which is to be found on page 3D23-0437 of the Croatian; and for the English it is 3D23-0847 and onwards until the 48th meeting. Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have enumerated all the meetings from the 25th of January, 1991, in Belgrade, the first meeting, all the meetings between Tudjman and Milosevic, the first one being the 25th of January, 1991, in Belgrade. I think that this meeting in the Villa Dalmacija was held on the 28th of March, that is to say, before the meeting in Karadjordjevo, so I think there's a mistake there. But I'm not quite sure about that, it's too far away in time now for me to remember exactly. But, anyway, Your Honours, I don't have the time to go through all the 48 meetings, but I'd just like to say that this gives a good clear review of them, when and where they were held, who took part in them, and what was said. Of the 48 meetings, at 31 of them Mr. Izetbegovic took part. And in four meetings where this question of the Bosnian partition was discussed, Stjepan Mesic took part. So apart from taking part, he was also well informed. And I can say nothing else but to state that enormous efforts were made for these meetings held in 1991 to arrive at a solution to the problem, but unfortunately there was no solution because, let me repeat this, was the Serbian plan -- Serbian political plan for Serbia to stretch along these lines [indicates], and I'll point to this on the map. These are the western borders of Serbia [indicates], and that's where Karlobag is. So this part of Croatia [indicates] can go, and everything to the east of that would be Yugoslavia. And I have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, General Praljak was looking at the map and pointing at the map, and I see that the Judges were not focusing on that. So perhaps General Praljak could again demonstrate with the map so we have a record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It would even be preferable, Mr. Praljak, if you could verbally be as precise as possible so that we have it in the record, because the record will not, itself, show where your hand and your pointer go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, then, the western borders of Serbia, as they were developed over the centuries and appeared in 1986 in the SANU memorandum and Milosevic's politics, according to that, all countries east of the Croatian border, all land east of the Croatian border, Virovitica, Karlovac, Karlobag, everything east of that would be Yugoslavia, including the entire region of Dalmatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and Montenegro and Macedonia. And Milosevic did not want to share that with anybody. Had he wanted to, I assume they would have agreed on that in 1991. So all of Croatian territory except perhaps for this area that they were prepared to let go [indicates], which was a fifth or a sixth of Croatia, not to be within Yugoslavia or Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Once again, General, let's remind the Court, although we began with this topic. After March 1991, what happened in the Republic of Croatia, after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, large Serbian rallies began to be held in Knin, Obrovac, Glina. All the emissaries came in from Serbia. Chetnik cockades were worn, and an uprising was raised, and Croatia was intensively preparing for a war at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did the war begin?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And we've shown that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They put up logs to block the main road running from Split to Zagreb. They put up logs which prevented the tourists from passing. And I, who was coming back from the coast at that time, was going via Bosnia and Banja Luka, because you couldn't go from Split to Zagreb across Croatia anymore because of these obstacles that had been erected in the form of logs and rocks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I heard you commenting on the 48 meetings that were held between Milosevic and Tudjman. The meeting in Karadjordjevo took place on the 25th of March, 1991. If, in fact, what is alleged actually happened, some kind of secret agreement was concluded, why is it, then, that this was not mentioned again three days later on the 28th of March, and then again two weeks later on the 4th of April in Belgrade, and then again on the 11th of April, and so on and so forth, unless all of this remained between the two of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
