utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, you can make the same conclusion yourselves, just like I can. There was no agreement, because had there been -- well, my testimony follows my logic. If they had reached an agreement, what would have been the purpose of all these other meetings, then? If you assume that the two of us reach an agreement, and we're rulers, well, what do we need the other people in the hall here for, in the courtroom? We have decided, we have might and power on our side, so why would we need all these other 30- or 40-odd meetings, or however there were subsequently, if that had been the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti, please allow me to say something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. I have an issue with the translation. On line 1 of page 51, in English it says "entirely secret." I had said "between face to face, between two individuals." If it's entirely secret, other people could be present. I wanted to correct the transcript. What is it you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me give you a bit of history. When Hitler and Stalin decided to divide up Poland, they did so. When Chamberland and Hitler reached an agreement on how England and the others wouldn't meddle in taking Czechoslovakia and Austria, he took Czechoslovakia and Austria. And I could quote hundreds of agreements like that. When two powerful people reach an agreement, they act upon it, and then they don't need to meet further, whereas this is quite senseless. I do apologise, but that's my testimony. It's a subsequent political settling of accounts that took place afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That is an opinion. That is not testimony. It's purely hypothetical, just a conjecture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, when did the war begin in the Republic of Croatia, the war with the JNA and Serbian Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, straight away at the start of the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And where did the fighting take place? We've already shown that, but let's hear it once again.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: The war began -- the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia was overthrown when, in the spring -- or, rather, late spring, when the police forces of the Republic of Croatia set out for Knin to deal with the traffic situation there, then the JNA aeroplanes forced helicopters, police helicopters, to go back on pain of them being shot down, and thereby this -- this was tantamount to an act of aggression against Croatia. And in one of my books, I give the exact date. I say how the helicopters were intercepted by the JNA. So that is an aggression. The army intervened against the police forces of a sovereign republic, and they could not have done that under the Yugoslav Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That was in 1990, was it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1990, when, according to how I see matters, the aggression against Croatia started, because in Yugoslavia the republican police forces had power over their own republican territory, and the JNA, when the police wanted to intervene towards Knin and allow the traffic to start functioning normally and to prevent the unrest there, should not have intervened. The Yugoslav Army said, You can't do that. That, as far as I was concerned, was the beginning of the aggression against Croatia which later on developed gradually as it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In the meetings that were held between the six presidents and when they negotiated the manner in which Yugoslavia could be disbanded, can you tell the Court what position was taken by Serbian Montenegro, what position Croatia and Slovenia took, and what position Macedonia and Bosnia took? Can we clarify that once again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Slovenia and Croatia, at the beginning, agreed to a confederation of republics; that is to say, that all the republics of the former Yugoslavia should form a confederation, an association which would be a confederation within Yugoslavia. Montenegro and Serbia wanted to have the kind of Yugoslavia that I have explained, a sort of expanded Serbia, whereas Mr. Izetbegovic and Kiro Gligorov proposed something that was called an asymmetrical confederation, an asymmetric confederation or federation. In other words, this meant that Bosnia and Herzegovina and Macedonia should remain with Serbia and Montenegro within a federation, and that Slovenia and Croatia should be within a confederation with the other republics. So that was one of the proposals put forward. It was completely idiotic, but what can you do? People think up all sorts of things to avoid a war. So at least the Slovenes and Croats and Alija tried to avoid a war. How far they were successful and how far they had intelligent plans, well, we've all been witness to the outcome of those.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: How do you know all these facts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was very well versed politically, I read everything that there was to read, and I followed current events, because that was something that we were involved in daily, and it had to do with our fate and destiny.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think now we can put away this book and turn to document 3D02005. This is the "Hrvatski Vojnik."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the right soldier or "vojnik."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you tell me which one it is, though?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the copy. It's not the right interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. We'll leave that for some later time. General, discussing these conversations --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can -- I can explain it here, and then we'll show it later on. In "Hrvatski Vojnik," "Croatian Soldier," Your Honours, that big rally in Sisak on the occasion of the anniversary of the 1st Partisan Detachment in Europe, which happened to be in the territory of Croatia as well, Franjo Tudjman, and I did not point that out then, declared, and this was in 1993 -- he again gave his opinion about this so-called agreement in Karadjordjevo, and this was done before the Diplomatic Corps and all the other people present. And he said there, There was no agreement of any kind between me and Milosevic. And of course we will subsequently go back to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes. After the break, we'll give you the page numbers. General, let's just wrap up with this general situation, and then we will move on to some specific events. So I'd just like to ask you about the referendum that was held in Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 28th of February and the 1st of March, and what the circumstances were at the time when this referendum was held, why it was held, and what you personally knew about the referendum, and how the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina responded to this referendum, especially those of Croatian decent.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not go into the conversations that I heard of here about Livno form of the referendum, and so on and so forth. What I know is the following: The Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina were dissatisfied with the way the question was formulated, the question was adopted in the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be proclaimed a unified state -- a unique state, a single state, which was the condition for its international recognition according to the Badinter Commission. And I know the following: Even as the referendum was being prepared, Franjo Tudjman sent Slavko Degoricija, a man who was highly positioned in the Croatian government and who was usually the man -- the envoy -- Mr. Tudjman's envoy for discussions with Serbs, and he had over 100 meetings with the Serbs in Croatia in order to -- in search for a solution. So he sent this man to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was supposed to rally the Croatian people by asking -- calling on them to respond to the referendum and to circle the "Yes" answer. Second: On the first day of the referendum, not many Croats actually responded, and there was a danger that the referendum would fail. I know for a fact that Dr. Franjo Tudjman pleaded with the Catholic priests who were in this area in Bosnia and Herzegovina and who enjoyed great reputation among the Croatian people in this country, so he asked them to call on the people on the second day of the referendum in their masses, in the services they held in their churches, that they plead with the people to respond to the referendum, to go and circle the answer "Yes," the affirmative answer which was in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And that by -- through his political influence with the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he called on them to mobilise people to vote "yes" for an integral Bosnia and Herzegovina. In my view, the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in view of the way the question was couched at the referendum, which did not provide for the foundations of the government in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so they -- the people of -- the Croatian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina would not have responded to this referendum the way it was framed, the question was framed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And what would have happened if they did not respond to the referendum?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I leave it to you to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I can -- I would now like to see document 1 -- or, rather, 3D -- that's 3D02003. That was related to the "Croatian Soldier" magazine, and in English that's 3D31-0080. General, I believe we are done with the books. Could the usher now please provide the Capljina-Stolac binder or file to the honourable Chamber. I'm being warned that I should intervene. In the transcript, the English page of "The Croatian Soldier," that's number 3D02003, 3D40-0933. So now we will move on to your whereabouts in 1993, but just let me explain beforehand to the Trial Chamber. This portion of the testimony will relate to paragraph 7, 15, 25, 26, and 27 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm a bit lost. I don't know where you're heading, because you said, on page 57, line 2 following, that you would go to 3D02003. And then you talked about the Capljina binder, and then you ask about the whereabouts in 1993. Where are we going?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's my error because I speak too fast. I was going to move to a different topic -- I was going to move to a different topic, and then my colleague, Mr. Kovacic, gave me the number of "The Croatian Soldier" that was the reference of Mr. Praljak, where he said that it published the interview of Mr. Franjo Tudjman, where he said that he -- there was no mention of the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So then I mentioned this number 3D02003, which is actually a reference to "The Croatian Soldier." In other words, the document in the binder entitled "Croatian Soldier." And then I was asked to give the English page, which was a wrong number, and then I was told to correct this error, and that's how this whole confusion came about. But it's really my fault because I was too fast, and I will try to be as -- to speak as slowly as I can. Now we will move on to 1992 and the Capljina-Stolac binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We've already heard before and we've also presented evidence that in 1992, you came to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or, more specifically, to Herzegovina, so, General, could you please tell us when it was exactly that you came there, why did you come there, and what was the situation that you found when you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard. I don't know where to begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, let's begin by you telling us why you came to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me say this: In March, there was already information about the situation in Herzegovina and what the intentions of the Yugoslav People's Army were in regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that those intentions had already been formulated. The Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina were already setting up volunteer small units in villages in Mostar. That would have been in neighbourhoods and so on. Now, the information that I had, and I've already explained this before, was that all this together was insufficiently organised in order to stop the advance of the Yugoslav People's Army according to the plans that I showed before, the plans drawn up by General Cokic, but others have also mentioned this and talked about it. I talked about this with Gojko Susak, the minister of defence, whom I met with briefly in the evening around 8.30, after we finished all the other -- the day's work. We met on these occasions as friends and not as superior and subordinate. And the information that he had was such -- it was more rosy, it was rosier, and that's because people usually present to their bosses in that part things in rosier shades than they really were. And that's how we went on for a couple of days, but I kept saying, The situation is not good. They will break through towards Split, towards Ploce. We won't be able to defend ourselves. And at one point I decided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Praljak. You mentioned the month of March. This is March 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said something earlier. You said that in the small villages, there were volunteer Croats that had set up small units. As you know, the Judges went to all these locations and we visited these villages. Were these formations set up spontaneously, people did this of their own accord, or were they obeying orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I know, Your Honour, there was no order. These were individuals. In Ljubusko, for instance, people gathered, people of similar beliefs, and I know they took them for training to the coast and then brought them back. There were nine, they called them battalions, whereas in terms of numbers, they were not even platoons. So there were some units in Ljubusko, in Radisici, some in Grude. And the HOS, the Croatian armed forces, were actually the forces best organised, but they were an army of a political party, the Croatian Rights Party. And they had their units until Franjo Tudjman ordered, because they even had a building in Zagreb which was secured and guarded by armed guards, and they had to disarm them by force. So there was no strength and no time, and especially not in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to establish an organisation that could in any way be comparable to an orderly armed force of any Western state.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Speaking of orderly armed forces, General, could you tell us what the situation was between various towns when you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will tell you about it, and you can interfere when you feel you need to. So when I arrived in the area, there was a Croatian officer with me, Crnjac. He hailed from those parts, and that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we have to explain how you happened to go there. Were you sent by the minister of defence, or did you go of your own accord? We have to say that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we weren't sent by the minister of defence. We went there voluntarily, of our own free will. I think there is no need to repeat this, but there could be no orders sending a Croatian soldier -- any Croatian soldier to a foreign territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But you could have been sent there to inform of the situation there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that could not be the case. Let me tell you this: My mother and father lived there, my sister lived in Sarajevo with two children and a husband, I also had a number of relatives there as well, and in addition not only these people, the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what would happen is they would actually reach the border of Dalmatia and we wouldn't be able to defend ourselves. So I think we don't have to do it this way. It's very elementary. We don't have to behave as if this was an elementary school. So there was one enemy, and this was one theatre of war and one defence, and their intentions were absolutely clear, and that's, I assume, a fact. So we returned, and then I informed of my visit. Franjo Tudjman, I said to him, Mr. President, they will break apart Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if we go on like this, they will also break up Croatia. So I proposed that he let me and General Crnjac, who was from those parts, and General Roso, to go there as volunteers and help organise the defence, because otherwise we would be expelled and murdered not only in Bosnia and Herzegovina but also in Croatia. And you can see easily, if you look at the border here [indicates], they had already been -- they had already taken control over what they called the military Krajina, so I did not see how we could put up a defence. He agreed with this, and I went there as a volunteer, and on the 10th of April, 1992, I took over the Operational Zone of South-Eastern Herzegovina, which is the territory from the River of Neretva from Konjic up to Capljina and the border with Croatia. I first arrived in Capljina, and now I can describe the situation. The situation was what is called in the sociology of society quite simply chaos, complete chaos from what normally functions in a normal state; electricity, traffic, bus routes, the police and whatever. There was none of that. There was something that in social psychology is called hysteria. Hysteria was prevalent. People wanted to do something, but nobody knew what it was that they wanted to do. And some lines were set up around Medjugorje, some small lines. The guys in Mostar defended their own districts. They destroyed Capljina. The JNA Army, and I've already said this, bombed towns, the towns of Siroki Brijeg, Grude, Citluk, Capljina, Ljubuski, killed civilians and children, and there you have it. And I arrived in Capljina in that kind of situation. There was a JNA barracks in Capljina, and behind Capljina, next to the village where I was born, in actual fact, and we began to defend ourselves. Now, what happened over there? The people of Ljubuski dug trenches. The Ljubuski municipality, Your Honours, dug trenches towards Medjugorje. Medjugorje dug trenches towards Ljubuski. In Siroki Brijeg, the commander or, rather, the president of some crisis staff or whatever was an artist, a painter, and they dug some trenches on the slopes of some hill. Complete chaos.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: There weren't any Serbs over there for them to be digging trenches. That's something the Judges don't know about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, why were they digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, each municipality closed itself off and were digging trenches facing each other. There was no communication, so you had to start from scratch and have your embryo and develop it. You have to be a psychologist, a mother, a father, a friend, a psychiatrist, to go first hot, then cold, and to develop this embryo as much as you could for it to shape into something that would be akin to some sort of organisation. For example, in Capljina, they brought in some guys by Radisa. They said, The Neretva River is there, you're behind the embankment. And then they forgot them for 48 hours. They left them without any water. The guys were 20 years old. They hadn't been in the Yugoslav People's Army. They were standing there for two days, hungry, thirsty, quite exhausted and beside themselves, waiting to see the 6th American Fleet turn up. And the only thing that you could feel as being the crystallisation of something was their desire and will to fight. But how were they to fight? That's the question. And I'll give Their Honours an example from the Franco-Turkish wars, and this is it: A Turk, fighting against two French soldiers, was victorious. Ten French soldiers was equal to 10 Turkish soldiers; but 100 French soldiers would vanquish 200 Turkish soldiers. And this an important principle in a war. Organisation is vital, how to set up the army's organisation, because if you have chaos, you cannot rule and you cannot perform in chaos. And as I say, for at least 20 hours a day, I would be working, touring all the positions, talking to the people, manning them and everybody else. And the staff was like a waiting room at a station, railway station. People were coming and going. Someone would come in and say that his house had been destroyed through shelling. People came in with all sorts of problems. It wasn't any army command or army staff; it was just a general help bureau, sort of thing. And as I say, there was hysteria, and the general view that suddenly prevailed was that we should give signs to the opposite side. For example, if a car was going uphill, you would see a reflection of their lights, so they were giving these signs to the Serbs. And then they arrested a relative of Bruno Stojic. Some policeman managed to catch him in Citluk and said that he was giving signs to the opposite side. And I went to intervene and asked them, Well, tell me, who was he signalling to, what kind of signs was he sending out, what kind of signals? Nobody had any idea. There was no rational explanation for any of this. But there was hysteria, and hysteria doesn't need rational explanations. Anyway, someone from the civilian police force remembered that you weren't allowed to drive around with your lights on at night. And as I drove around visiting my units in this area fairly frequently, I drove around at night, suddenly they would jump out at a certain point and ask me why I was driving around with my lights switched on, with my headlights on. And then I would stop and say, I am deep within Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what's that got to do with my headlights being on? Who cares about whether they're on or not? The artillery uses charts to fire their -- fire at their targets. You have planes flying overhead. We have no capacity to aim against those planes. But of course this is all social psychology, and individuals in this historical, chaotic situation quite simply become completely irrational people; not everyone, of course, but the vast majority. The vast majority of people were completely lost, and you have to take it step by step to use your energy and knowledge and harness this to deal with the situation. Now, you also have to raise your level of organisation, because you can't, Your Honours, issue an order that nobody's going to respect and act upon. Then your respect would have been destroyed. And even if you wrote down an order, there was nobody to implement those orders. Now let me give you another example, a command -- army command from Capljina, for example. It deployed to four or five kilometres outside Capljina, because they thought they would control somebody over there, but they had nobody to manage and control over there. And I replaced that entire setup, that entire command, because what had happened, in fact, is that they had fled. You have to be there, and if you're killed, you're killed. So it's an organisation that you had to create rather than manage. You had to take it from man to man, from hour to hour, from day to day, from one part of the territory to another, patiently and with all the knowledge you can muster. Secondly, there was no telephone communication between Citluk and Siroki Brijeg. I told them to set up a line there so I could have this communication at all times, and at one point I picked up the telephone receiver, although the line had been cut. I sent two guys to go and see what had happened, where the line was cut. And they returned, and their explanation was that, We checked the situation up, up to our borders, and the line -- the communication line is all right there. Beyond that isn't our municipality. So I called them up to check that out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, telephone receiver.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I would like to make a correction to the transcript, because the sense is changed unless what General Praljak said is interpreted fully. On page 65, line 22, General Praljak said that he received an explanation according to which they had checked out the lines up until the borders of their municipality, and that they weren't interested in going further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct. Now, Your Honours, if these were normal times, I would sit these people down and say that a war -- you don't have municipalities separated in a war. I would talk to them, but -- and I would have been very angry. I would have shouted at them, slammed my fist on the table, broken some chairs and instilled fear into their bones. But I didn't have time to do all this. I didn't have six months to put some order into this. But through my reactions, I would react very strongly, and then I'd talk to them the next day and said that this wasn't personal, it's just that things like that couldn't be done that way. There are thousands of details and instances of that kind. It's difficult to explain to people who haven't been in a situation like that themselves. Well, I started with Citluk. Anyway, they said at the meeting 17 that they weren't going to go to war anymore until the money problem had been resolved. I set up -- I set the team up at 5.00 in the morning. I sent them off on a march. I shouted at them. I forced them to go. Then I talked to them calmly. I talked to them like a parent, not like their commander, because you had to bring them up like you bring up children. You had to educate them, train them. They were wonderful guys, young men who wanted to fight. But organisation is a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please slow down, because the record didn't reflect what you said in Citluk, that they wouldn't go to war until some problem had been solved. What was the problem?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Problem about money, some pay. Anyway, something completely irrelevant. Then you saw Mr. Buntic's position here. He was angry because of something over there, and he tendered his resignation. Resignation? He wanted to leave the army. He's a wonderful man, full of good qualities. But you can't tender your resignation in the middle of a war, so I pointed a gun and said, Go back to work. We've been friends for ten years, but now I'm telling you to go back to work. Well, I wasn't ready to actually shoot at him, but he couldn't know how far I was prepared to go and prevent him from making a fool of himself and handing in his resignation. Anyway, up until June we had an army which was ready and had liberated the right bank, although I was there for a far shorter period of time. I wasn't a legal commander for a long period of time. I was appointed and then relieved of my duties. Now, the other important thing is to look at the situation around the Capljina barracks. A situation that had to be solved was the JNA barracks in Capljina, the garrison there. Capljina, Grabovina, whatever. I talked to General Perisic at the time, on two or three occasions, I believe, and offered him a solution. I said that the army could leave Capljina quietly and slowly and that the officers could take their weapons with them, according to the book, the rules and regulations that I'd once read about how this should be done. He shouted over the phone, said he'd destroy everything, said he knew where I was hiding. He used a nickname, "Baco" or something like that. Anyway, all this was beyond any type of civilised exchange. And pursuant to the international agreement, people tried to pull out their husbands and children. A Serb tried to get his son out. A Muslim arrived from Bosnia. He was frightened for his child's life. There was several women whose husbands worked there as non-commissioned officers or officers and who lived around the barracks. Anyway, I wasn't able to reach an agreement with them and to have them leave the barracks in orderly fashion. The condition was that they should leave the weapons that were in the barracks. And after they had been taken over there were two tanks there, a lot of machine-guns, anti-aircraft cannons, single-barrel, double-barrel. I think there was a four-barrelled one as well. Anyway, the barracks -- Capljina was in the middle. The Serbs were on one side, across the Neretva River. Then the barracks were on the other side. They shot at one point. There was chaos in Capljina. And, Your Honours, when we're talking about all this and the chaos, I tested how I would obstruct the tanks from leaving, block the tanks. People were shooting at me in my back. The bullets lodged in the soil right beside my feet. Anyway, there were killers in town, the ones that had been in Sarajevo and so on. They killed civilians, these people. And after that, I said that all the blinds on all the windows must be lowered because, you see, there was nothing to stop retaliation. And that's enough of that. We can go on to discuss the barracks. If the Judges have any questions, I'm willing to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. If I understood you correctly, you organised everything as of March 1992. There is only one enemy, right, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the constitution -- in the way -- the formation that you're setting up, the military formation you're setting up, are there Croats and Muslims together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both. At the beginning, more Croats, and then after that there were more and more Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From your position, if I understand you correctly, you are alone and you're not receiving orders from anyone. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From no one, Your Honour. At that time, there was so much work to do, so many things to see to, that when General Petkovic arrived and when he became chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, I don't know whether we managed to see each other once at a meeting before June or whatever. There was nothing to receive, no orders to receive from anyone, nor could you issue any written orders, because you had nobody to issue the orders to. You had to create a piece of -- or have a piece of paper and then write things down. Everything was done orally, by word of mouth; first of all, on a human, friendly basis. Then you would shout. Then you would beg. Then you would try and use other methods. For example, in Capljina, a young guy arrived. He was from the area, himself, but he had been in Borovo Selo and Vukovar, and he was in the war there. He was a quiet young man. He used to live in Canada, in a civilised way. Anyway, I appointed him the commander of Capljina. His name was Luburic. And I handed out the lilies to the BH Army for them to carry as their emblem, so I brought him to that position. Then you had to think up a commander for Siroki Brijeg, because this painter who had been to the Academy of Arts had absolutely no clue as to how this was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. This is March 1992, you're setting everything --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in April now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, April 1992. Now, at the time the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised. In April, it had been recognised. So did you ever have the idea of trying to contact those who are in Sarajevo to say, I'm Praljak, and I would like to be under the command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you do that, actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I did not follow that path. Well, you will see there are other things I'll tell you, but you will see what the situation was in Sarajevo, and this is in the description of the Muslim leaders. They were barely able to save their own heads. We had no communication with Mostar at all. I was forced to enter Mostar on a road that was shelled from three different Serb positions, and they managed to actually hit my car on one road -- bend of the road. And, in fact, I travelled this road on a number of occasions, and they did not manage to hit me. I wasn't even able to reach Grude. I had no idea what was going on in Grude, let alone in Sarajevo. So there was absolutely no way of getting in touch with, let's say, Sarajevo. Secondly, there were -- there was no authority in Sarajevo. There was no government, there was nothing, because that was not even possible if you bear in mind how Alija Izetbegovic, the commander, behaved in this wartime situation, because three days earlier he had claimed that there would be no war. This was, simply put, an uprising, a self-organised popular uprising.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, did the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina exist in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You talked about the Grabovina barrack and you described what the situation was there, who was there, and under whose auspices, as it were, these people actually gathered there, the people whose members of family were within the barrack. We can show this in our video here, and that's 3D03131. The transcript was distributed, I believe, to everyone, and I would appreciate you to comment as we look at this video excerpt. You will also hear what's being said, and you can tell us who's being shown on the footage and what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Is this Capljina or Grabovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have the video image. All right, I have it now. This is Grabovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And this is the HVO Army; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This was in April 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Are these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them have rifles, some don't. These are just young men who got together. They didn't even have a commanding officer. These are women awaiting the outcome of that discussion or negotiation, because according to the agreement between the commander of this barrack and the European Monitors who were there at the time. So this was Luburic, the young man I appointed as commander. That's him. So these women, according to the agreement, were supposed to go and talk to -- and this here we see is Mr. Moro. So these women were supposed to go to the barracks gate. Of course, these people were used to something, and that's quite understandable, and that was that according to an agreement between the commanders of the armies, that this agreement would be honoured and that there wouldn't be any problem with them getting inside the barrack and seeing their family members. But, of course, I knew that it didn't work that way with the Yugoslav People's Army, so I sent Luburic and I was there too. I was around there somewhere too. I sent Luburic to monitor this, because I had good reason to assume that there will be at least some complications and that they might even kill someone. And if anyone did get killed, it was absolutely -- it was quite certain that it would -- that the HVO would be blamed for it. Now, believe me, I had an example of that type. The Swede, the colonel, who was the chief of the European Monitors at the time, at Cula, one of his men was killed. And when his men would the Yugoslav People's Army and saw the order there, the office and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, please, we apologise. We can see that you're here in the footage, so can you describe what's going on here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I came to see how this conversation, this negotiation, is going to go on, because I didn't believe that it would have a good outcome. Now, this is the road leading to the northern gate of the barrack. Could we just fast-forward? There's nothing to see here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately we can't do anything about it. This is electronics.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Well, will you stop that maniac with that rifle?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was a shot from the barracks that had already started. You can't hear it in the footage, and I was here calling on them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Will you check what the fuck who is that idiot there shooting at people and killing people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was actually -- well, I was actually swearing because they had come here for negotiations, and throughout this time, and we'll see it in a moment. Your Honours, I'm on the road, and since I'm mentioning my own role there, you can see that I'm a perfect target there. I was some 80 metres from the gate to the barrack, and I can just tell you that I was simply beside myself every time there was any kind of violation of any kind of rules. So here I am sitting there as a target, and I am telling him these were mothers of these men there and that he was a criminal. He was a criminal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that idiot, whoever was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you give us a name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name. How should I know that? Now, here you can see that's the gate to the barrack, Your Honour. You will see a little later this house that was already dilapidated because no one had lived there for a long time, this was the house of my late grandfather. I'll point it out later. You see -- and you'll see here this is one of these women -- could you please just stop here. This is the moment where even the person who was filming this did not dare go out and film it. When they reached the gate, this idiot shot at these people, and these people fell to the ground. They threw themselves on the ground. I went there to help them get up, and I escorted them back, and I was a clear target then. Now, throughout all this, these people, this gentleman, Mr. Moro, and these women and so on, they've given a statement to this Tribunal regarding these events. And when I refer to those statements I will only do that to avoid talking about myself, but rather to allow you to hear the statements that are authentic, and their only reason for giving those statements was to establish the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And I will just ask for you to allow us to read these statements, because they will significantly contribute to describing and explaining what the situation was. Now you can see here this is the gate, the entrance to the barrack. The barrack is some 70 metres away. Now you can see in what kind of mental state these people were. By the way, in this house on the right-hand side, in this room there -- so they shot at these people. These people threw themselves to the ground. And, Your Honours, I went to help them get out of there, in my full size and presence, and I'm not a small man. And that’s a 14 contribution to the portrait of Slobodan Praljak the criminal. Although this gentleman here, he's a Serb, and the husbands of these women, they were employed by the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And they were within the barrack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They went to see them. We can wrap up here. There's nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, General. But you began your sentence, and you never 21 finished it. You said that on the right-hand side there is a house and this 22 room where – what? And then you were interrupted. What were you going to say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since you mentioned it, my mother was at Vis. She was with the partisans. She fell in love with my father there, I guess, and got pregnant, and she was sent back to give birth here in my grandfather's and grandmother's house, and this is the house in which I was born. Well, this is just a detail to also give you some detail that's not really too important.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What do you mean, it's not important?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why would it be important? It's just literature, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to interrupt you here. You mentioned the Swedish representative, and you said that he was at Cula. Could you please tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a representative of the European community was killed by the Yugoslav People's Army at Cula. However, when a member of a regular army, Sweden in this case, comes to the premises of the Yugoslav People's Army to see Perisic or whoever, what he can see is that there is a regular army there. They salute, there's order, and so on. So when these people tell him that his men had been killed by the HVO, and then when he comes to see me and sees my troops and my soldiers, of course he would believe the orderly army. So I had to take this gentleman to the place where our positions were, to show him that spot. Then I went with him to the spot where his man had been killed, and again I showed him the Serbian positions which were about 120 metres from there, and I explained to him that there was no chance, in theory even, that we could have shot this man. But the only way to actually prove this is to take the man there, to tell him, Let's go there, and then I will expose myself to their fire too, because this man -- such a man, whenever he's -- when he saw us, we -- in his mind, we were a sort of renegade group. I don't even know what word to use here, some paramilitary troops. Some people had rifles; some didn't. They were not -- they were disorderly in clothes. They didn't even know how to keep in rank and file. But I understand his position. It's not that he was untruthful. He just was not prepared to understand the situation in which he found and we found ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to stop now because of the break, and we are reaching the end of the tape, so we have need to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question to put to you. We've seen you on the video, Mr. Praljak. We saw you talking to the JNA, through live speaker. We saw the women. Mr. Moro who was accompanying you. We saw this. But on seeing this, aware of the chaos you described to us in Capljina, I was wondering the following: How is it that a man, who is alone, starts interfering in complicated problems - the JNA, the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina - without any mandate to do so and on a purely personal basis? Did you believe that you alone would be able settle this situation, which was extremely complicated? I'm basing all of this on the video, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how shall I answer that? From the 10th of April, 1991, 'til the 7th of May -- what, what do you say? Yes, 1992, that's right. From the 10th of April, 1992, to the 7th of May, 1992, I was officially the commander of the territory I was in. And then on the 7th of May, I handed over my duties and went back to Croatia, because I was a volunteer and there was a lot to do over there in my department. Anyway, to answer your second question now. Your Honours, somebody has to. Now, who's going to be that person? If there's no organisation set up, then somebody has to say something. Of course, you don't know where it's going to lead and how successful you're going to be, but have you to start somewhere. If you don't start, you're not going to develop. And as you were able to see, until the beginning of July -- rather, in June, this resulted in the fact that in a very short space of time, young men like this, of the kind you saw, managed to set up units that managed to liberate the right bank of the Neretva River and the left bank, and Stolac as well, and this was in the space of just two and a half months. On the 7th of May, as I said, I went back to Zagreb. I gave back everything I was issued and went back to Zagreb. But quite literally, I went down there -- escaped down there and went down there whenever I could. I would get into my car, switch the engine on, drive myself, leave at 4.00 in the afternoon, leave Zagreb at 4.00 p.m., and arrive there around midnight, do my work down there, help out the young men there and the guys. I would take in refugees from Stolac and then get back into my car and drive all the way back to Zagreb. And to be quite honest, I didn't inform Gojko Susak about that, let alone Franjo Tudjman. So that's the truth of it. Now, how you're going to assess all this and what theory you're going to devise to incorporate those facts, I don't know, but I'm telling you what the facts are as they stand. You have to take the leap. Like the frog, you jump -- the optimistic frog. You jump into a bowl of milk, you swim 'round and 'round until you form some butter, and they you get out that way. And you work for over 20 hours. I was both a general and a sergeant, and I said I was the organiser, the father and mother and what have you. I was everything, and sometimes very roughly. And may we go into private session for me to give you an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Witness, in light of what we've heard and what we've seen, we are able to realise that you are somebody involved in a number of fields, in a number of research fields. You are a sociologist, and you were a military man also, a very learned man. There's something that's bothering me ever since I've seen this video depicting the events in Capljina, showing your intervention there. During combat, the heads of the military are usually seeking shelter because they still have to be in command, and if that's not the case, the morale of the men diminishes. You are there, standing with your loud-speaker, and you are facing the snipers. The question I have for you is this: Were you aware of the fact, precisely because there was chaos, that these famous snipers could hit you and that would put an end to this operation which you had prepared? In other words, you wanted to save the situation, and then you would be a martyr? You wanted to take control of the village, which was the village of your ancestors. Is there any military or sociological grounding for the way you behaved on that day or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Mindua, yes, I can. Had I in any way been able to sit in the staff office of a general, if there was a proper army with commanding officers and so on, I would write down my orders and the orders would be carried out. But the group of people that I had to deal with, the one you saw, was not that kind of army. It wasn't that level of organisation which would allow for officers to be -- orders to be taken over, the kind of orders that you're talking about. These people were shot at, at the very gates. They fell to the ground, so I can't expect these young men to go there and pick them up. Now, whether I was going to be killed or not, not only then but before in Sunja and in other places, I paid absolutely no attention to that because at that moment it's what had to be done. I didn't even think about it, about this...let’s call it morals. It’s just a need of my body and mind. I didn't give it any thought at that moment. I just did what had to be done because I was angry, I was bitter. I was angry at the idiot shooting, the result being that five or six people were lying down on the ground, women, children -- women or whatever. So I went to pick them up. That's the only thought that guided me at that moment, to pull them out and take them to shelter. I know how to organise people, but I'm fairly lazy. Nothing interested me but books. But if an organisation is in place, then I would know how to manage that organisation and I would say, You do that, you do this, and so on. But that was just not possible. You had to do something, you had to act and react, and then issue orders gradually, little by little. And that was what happened from time to time. Mr. Luburic, for example, became a commander as time went by, and then some young men appeared and they managed to effect control over some units, and then you could issue an order to Mr. Luburic, and then he would be placed between me and that unit, in between the -- the go-between man, the middleman. But otherwise, up until that time, that was just impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... because your army or your troops were in the making, and you were angry and you were altruistic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, now this story about the barracks hasn't been fully told yet. We saw you standing in front of the barracks, and how did it all end, this taking over of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to say something that I've already said here, and it's this: The only unit which at that point in time, apart from some young men from Radisici and Ljubuski and a HOS company led by Mr. Primorac, once again thanks to the personality that he was, he managed to form what could be said to be an army, and it was part of The King Tomislav unit, Daidza's unit, that is, and that unit was up at Citluk, Tepcici, Slipcici, and I pulled that unit out to help us in the liberation of the barracks and in taking control of the barracks. And to replace him, these 160 people came from the 4th Guards Brigade, which covered that territory, and they were there for some time. Now, this young man later became a well-known commander, and he had been to the Military Academy. He was a young officer graduating from the Academy, from the Yugoslav People's Army, and he asked to be given an area of responsibility. He asked me for that. So I said -- well, these guys had already fought in the war in Croatia, that this would weaken his left and right flank, so I demanded that he deploy his men -- have five or six of his men, then five or six locals, or twenty locals, or however many. And at a certain point in time when he thought that -- well, when the locals told me they were ready to take up their zones, in the first Chetnik attack where the locals were deployed, they -- four young men from Ljubuski were killed. So that's a lot for one small place. Later on, people become accustomed to the wounding and the killing, but four was a lot. So I said, you see, mistakes like that are paid for with people's 18 lives. So I gave in and, although I was doubtful, but they all agreed that 19 they were ready. That's just a small detail. Now, the barracks -- well, there 20 was shooting from the barracks. There were dead civilians. We lost about 21 seven or eight men, and there were over twenty others who were wounded. 22 General Perisic made the right military move, because he used helicopters in 23 the valley of a river, and he had them fly low behind a Roman camp, 24 Mogorjelo, and land within a playing field in the barracks -- within the 25 barracks compound. And people -- soldiers from the barracks got into the 1 helicopters, but 30 men remained. Now, although this landing, there was a 2 whole cannonade -- artillery cannonade at Capljina, 11 planes were used to 3 bomb Capljina, there were tanks firing from the left bank with recoilless 4 guns, tanks and so on. All hell broke loose. There was an all-out artillery 5 attack. Hundreds and hundreds of projectiles were used. I ordered the 6 people not to shoot at those helicopters, Let the people leave, let them 7 board the helicopters and leave. Now, the 30 men who remained surrendered, 8 and we took them captive, and then I recounted all this. So, Judge Mindua, I attended to semesters of social psychology, and I attended a few semesters in psychology and so on. How could I assume that after all the suffering in Herzegovina and the victims, it might be possible for one or two people to appear who wanted revenge, wanted to take their revenge? And that is why I stuck to those guys. I didn't move away from those young men, and I said, Find some buses. Well, it was difficult to find buses. First of all, I had to find people who might know where some bus might be, be had, and then I asked them to search for that bus. And then I talked to the owner, because who was going to guarantee that he was going to get his bus back, because we expected the barracks to be bombed again by Perisic. But, anyway, it's true and correct that two men appeared who wanted to take their revenge against the soldiers. I'm not going to show Your Honours what my meeting with them was like. Well, I took out my pistol, I cocked it, placing it into their mouths, and the maddest person 24 wins, the most audacious, and my face of a madman and what I carried within 25 me prevailed. I was victorious. I managed to get the better of these two guys. So I sent them to Metkovici, and they went via Croatia to Hungary, and then from Hungary they went back to their homes, and that's how they went to the other side. You can ask me what happened to those two men. All I can say is I don't know. I didn't have the strength to disarm them because I was no longer sure whether they would have handed over their weapons, and then there would have been a shooting match. Anyway, at that point in time you concentrate your mind on saving the people that needed to be saved. Of course, the normal thing would be for somebody to take them prisoner and to take legal proceedings against them ultimately, but at that point in time I was the person there, and I couldn't let them get away with it. Now, one of the doctors who was in the barracks, the young man Moro, he stayed on in the HVO, and he was a doctor in the Capljina Brigade. He became an HVO soldier, major, and all the rest of it. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In Grabovina, the Zurovci who lived there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you saw that village only partly. There was a Serb settlement called Zurovac. From my late grandfather, with whom I spent about two or three weeks of every summer holiday, I heard about those people, I knew of them. I knew old Damjan and others. And at one point, I was told, after all the dead in Capljina and the losses in the barracks, that some people burst in and that they wanted to kill them because they found some weapons on them. Through a very fast intervention, I was able to send men, and we removed those people. After that, I heard from some lads from the village, that they were willing to guard the hamlet together with the Serbs, and I charged them with that task, and I went to talk to the Serbs. I told them that it would not be possible -- there were a lot of Serbs in Capljina. They were not the only ones. I told them that it would not be possible and nobody should take the responsibility for that, especially when I was gone. How should I know when -- who would be guarding them after that? So I spoke to the younger ones and told them to either join the HVO, where they would be protected with a group, because their peers would protect them, or, B, to go across Croatia to Hungary, and then from Hungary to Serbia, and to leave the elderly behind and those who so wanted. That would have been their choice. This was my advice, and that advice concerned the realistic impression of the situation. It didn't have anything to do with the legal formulations and my desire, because I knew what I would have wanted at the time. However, the primary concern was for people not to lose their lives, because everything else was just empty talks. What benefit would somebody have if people were placed on trial for having killed them? They would have been dead. So some people left Zurovac in that way, and later on they contacted me. And some elderly gentlemen and ladies stayed behind until the end of the war, and finally they provided statements for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When we were talking about Capljina and the barracks there, and the operation to liberate the barracks, you mentioned a HOS unit. Did you have any problems with the HOS in that area, in the area of Capljina and thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem with the HOS existed at the time because the HOS commander, Mr. Kraljevic, was -- first of all, we're talking about two different militaries, so if somebody has a discipline issue in the HVO and you want to punish them, they moved to the HOS, and vice versa; somebody does something in the HOS and they move to the HVO. I had problems talking to Kraljevic. I had some painful meetings with him. But at that time he had a lot of troops under his command, and that problem obviously -- you know what? There were a lot of fantastic guards there, fantastic combatants. For example, this particular unit and this guy, Stanko Primorac, who became the commander of the Ljubisa Brigade in 1993 after Ivo Tomic was wounded, those were supreme combatants, and they had a wonderful organisation. However, there was a lot of scum there, people who would have committed crimes, who plundered and looted and were renegades, as it were. In September 1993, Blaz Kraljevic, with seven of his men --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 1992. He was killed somewhere between Mostar and Citluk, and it was a huge problem. I arrived from Zagreb very soon after that, and until the month of March 1993, we were all dealing with this problem. It was a major, major problem because some HOS units, especially those from Stolac, wanted to involve in a show-down with some of the HVO units. Stojic was also involved, and Petkovic, Prkacin as well, who was a HOS general based in Zagreb. Mate Boban was also involved. Stanko Primorac as well. And as for this particular group and all that, I played a role. Stanko Primorac writes about all that, because those lads held me in high esteem. And I would put myself between them or among them, especially in view of the fact that the HOS started receiving a huge number of Muslims who then took up arms, and then they would transfer to the BiH Army, and they also established some units that consisted exclusively of the Muslims, and their politics was absolutely unclear. This party, the HSP, that was the umbrella organisation for the HOS, that party spoke about the Croatian state all the way up to the Drina River. For that party, the Muslims were Croats of Islamic religion, so it remains unclear to this very day to me how come that Alija Izetbegovic and some other commanders of the BH Army supported such a political and military option. The problem with the HOS was discussed at a number of painstaking meetings. Obviously, some HOS groups remained in Zenica and Mostar. Some were incorporated by the BiH Army. We saw some documents issued by Arif Pasalic to that effect. However, as the HVO is concerned, this problem was solved in the spring of 1993. And now that we're talking about this, sometime in September or the beginning of October 1992, one group of the HOS members had a camp for Serbs in Dretelj, and I learned about that in one way or another. Somebody told me. I can't remember who because the events followed each other in a very quick succession. And then I spoke to Zare Pavlovic, who I met in Capljina, and he was a member of the military police at the time. And I told him to prepare people because I'd been told that ugly things were happening over there. I told him to prepare his men. And I repeat again, Your Honours, at that point I did not have any official appointment, any mandate to do anything. This was my own will. I did it of my own free will, whatever I did. Nobody from the HZ-HB objected or complained, Stojic or Petkovic. Everybody knew that I would be coming there to work. I took full responsibility for what I was doing. I did my job. I reported on what had happened. I reported both to Petkovic and Stojic and whoever, and then I returned. But let me continue where I left off. Obradovic, who was the brigade commander, I spoke to him and I told him to place two PATs across the road from the camp, and I sent Pavlovic there to tell the HOS members that they should hand the people -- the inmates over to me, or I would start shooting. And when I said I would start shooting, I meant killing. Either I would be given those men, the inmates from the camp, or I would start opening fire on the HOS who were there. You know, the shooting never materialised, because when the opposing side shows you flexing muscles and your determination to act, that scum, and it's usually scum that does that, they withdraw because they are weak. Whatever they do, they do it because they're weak, they're scum, not because they're strong and powerful and mighty. Obviously, I prepared buses. I had done it one day earlier. I prepared buses, as I'm saying, and I took the prisoners from the camp. I transported them to the barracks in Capljina, and the story goes on along the same way. I told them either to stay put and avoid foreign exchange, or if they didn't want to do that, that they should go to Croatia and then to Hungary, and then on to Serbia, which bordered on Hungary. I mean, they were given free hands to go wherever they wanted to go. So this is the whole story which I have made short.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you now look at document 5D00 --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What PD? 3D, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: No, 5D. This is at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. I would like to correct a mistake in the transcript. On page 89, line 25, the general said, "I told them either to wait to be exchanged," and in the transcript what we read is "foreign exchange."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told them either to stay there and wait to be exchanged or, if they didn't want to do that, there was no way for me to let them go to -- there was nowhere for them to go. So alternatively, they were advised to go to Croatia, so some of them opted for the first option, the others opted for the second option.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 5D00477, to round off our story about the HOS. This is a document that has already been admitted into evidence in this case. This was issued by the Ministry of the Interior, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution Order of the Republic of Croatia, and the document is dated 15th of October, 1992. And the subject of the document is the activities of the Security Services of the HOS and the potential -- a silent liquidation. General, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a correction in the transcript. Line 17, the number is 5D00447. One "4" is missing here, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is 5D00477.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General -- 5D00477. General, the circumstances described in the document -- do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The circumstances described in the document regarding the behaviour of that group for silent liquidations and the events, or things done by some HOS members, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after the killing of Blaz Kraljevic and the shooting that resulted in that, and obviously after that the HOS, as an organisation, was struck with chaos. I can't testify about that first-hand. However, what I know is that a HOS unit from Stolac, which comprised of over 90 percent Muslims, wanted to engage in a show-down with the HVO. I participated in that event, together with Mr. Primorac, who was also a HOS member. However -- or let me put it this way: In the HOS, there were a lot of good boys, honest men, good fighters, but there was a lot of scum, thieves, thugs, dark characters, seedy characters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, General, who was this document sent to? And you will find it on the last page, page 5, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the head of the office, Mr. Manolic; to the minister of the internal affairs, Mr. Jarnjak; and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. And you -- when you were talking freely about the events in the territory of Capljina and Stolac municipalities in the year 1992, you mentioned the fact that you were engaged in the receipt of refugees from the territory of Dubrava, Bivolje Brdo, and the territory around Stolac. What can you tell us about that, please? Please be very specific.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that a lot has been said about that. A lot has been said about the Serb conquest of Stolac, how people were fleeing before the Serbs. However, what is true can be summed up in two details. You saw from some of the previous testimonies that some Muslims established good relations with the Serbs and that they did not want to fight for Stolac at the very outset, and that people from the HVO, who were willing to defend Stolac, were standing in their way, and that's why they forbade them to dig trenches in their fields, which resulted in a lot of embitterment among some people. Furthermore, there were rumours, and I don't know if they were true. But according to the rumours, some Muslims, when the Serbs entered Stolac, were ready to meet them with flowers, the Serbs. I don't know whether this information is true or not. However, when there are rumours of the kind, you have to invest a lot of effort in order to calm the situation down. There is one more thing. The hodja from Capljina testified here, and I asked him -- he delivered a speech earlier on, and during that public speech he spoke about Jihad with the best of intentions. Your Honours, Jihad, in its original sense, is not a sacred war. Jihad is just a road that every Muslim has to travel during their lifetime in order to come closer to their god or, rather, Allah. On that road, they have to be good, honest, virtuous, and so on and so forth. So this is a positive thing, like the Catholics have to do. They have to respect their religion. However, when you say something like that in a public meeting -- and then I asked the gentleman who was here, I asked him that. Of course, nobody will understand such analyses, such layman's analyses. A lot of people over there understood his words in the wrong standard way, as Jihad being something that imposes a war upon them. They thought that they had to start waging a war against everything that was non-Islamic. So such things had to be calmed down, and it's impossible to tell the whole story with all the details, it's absolutely impossible to relay such a situation. I'm just giving you some details of some situations, and I repeat, 20 hours a day I would tour every position, twice a day I would do that, I would talk to every single soldier. I had hundreds of conversations, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And to document 3D02639 now, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, you do. It's at the beginning, before the table, 02639, and it's excerpts from Suad Cupina's book. It's at the beginning of your binder.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say, 02639? Right, I've found it. 25 Q. "Treason and the BiH Defence 1991-1995" and we're interested in 3D33-0360. And for the English, it is 3D40-1175. They are two short excerpts, if I can call them that, from the book "Betrayal," in which Mr. Cupina says what you've just been saying. It's about how the Capljina barracks were taken control of and about the situation in the Capljina municipality area. And it is his position, according to these excerpts, that there was an agreement struck between the Croats and the Serbs, linked to the situation in the Neretva River valley. May I have your comments, since your name is mentioned here as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've chosen this as an example of something that I want to illustrate and explain. The author of this book and his brother lived in Aleksa Santic Street in Mostar, one storey and a flat above my flat; the same building, the same entrance. They were younger, but I knew them ever since childhood. First of all, I personally provided this individual with weapons for the Muslims or the BH Army in Mostar. That's the first point. Secondly, this same man was a karate specialist and had medals and so on. Now, Mr. Cupina, with Mr. Sulejman Budakovic, who was the deputy to Arif Pasalic, and the third man, Daidza, the third Muslim, was sitting in Vrgorac in Croatia. They were in Croatia, in Vrgorac, and commenting, in his small karate expert's mind, and said that Anton Tus had received an expression of gratitude from Perisic because we had ten people dead and over twenty people injured. Furthermore, he knows what Bobetko was doing. And then he goes on to say, They are waiting to see the outcome of the battle to have Praljak, Tus, and Perisic reach an agreement so that they can take over all the resources and means for the Independent Mostar Battalion. Now, it's very important, Your Honours, to see the line of thinking of a man like this, of this calibre. So you have three Muslims sitting in Croatia, waiting for Praljak to finish taking over the barracks, so that they can be given weapons for the Mostar Battalion, and then they go on to construe a Tus-Perisic conversation about that. And he goes on to say that Bozan's unit entered Capljina but that I sent it back. So you can't have more lies than that or a more vulgar way of thinking. That is an insult to my very soul and intellect. You cannot conceive of anything beyond that. But it testifies to the fact that a number of Muslims felt themselves to be the masters, for which we had to take control of the barracks and then they can tell any story they wanted, and that was not the only instance of this. There were people that thought along those lines, and this led to numerous misunderstandings, because if Bozan's men saw that, it would be difficult to prevent a brawl, because that's all it merits, a brawl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
